The **TR-909 bass drum** is a *hybrid* design: a pitched oscillator with a short downward **pitch envelope** for the body, plus a separate **click/noise attack** layer and a longer **amplitude decay** for the tail.[3][4][8] In practical synthesis terms, the “sound of the 909 kick” comes from a fast pitch sweep at the start, a relatively pure sine-like body, and a short transient click layered on top.[3][11]

## What the controls do

- **TUNE**: sets the pitch behavior of the bass drum’s oscillator by changing the starting pitch/sweep behavior of the pitch envelope, not just the steady-state pitch.[2][4][5]
- **ATTACK**: controls the amount/level of the initial click or noise burst, making the front edge sharper or softer.[2][3][4][10]
- **DECAY**: controls how long the bass drum rings out; turning it up lengthens the tail, turning it down makes it crisper.[4][8][10]

## Numeric description of the sound

The most specific number I found for the 909 kick’s pitch sweep in the gathered sources is that the **Tune** control affects a **short falling pitch envelope** with a **standard range of about 30 to 120 ms**.[2] That is the best explicit technical figure available in the sources retrieved here.

For the amplitude side, the sources state that **Decay** governs the kick’s overall length, but the gathered sources do **not** provide a single authoritative ms range for the factory 909 across all settings.[4][10] One technical write-up notes that the pitch-envelope decay can be stretched to about **4×** the usual range in a modded unit, which implies the stock range is intentionally fairly narrow.[5]

## Attack/click component

The TR-909 kick is not just a clean sine sweep; it has a **separate attack transient**. Sound On Sound describes the bass drum as a mixed composite: a pitched oscillator path plus a lower path made from noise and a **short pulse (essentially a click)**, both shaped by envelopes before being mixed together.[3] Roland’s own manuals also separate **Attack** and **Decay** as independent bass-drum controls.[4][8][10]

## TR-909 kick vs TR-808 kick

- **TR-808**: classic bass drum sound is commonly associated with a **bridged-T oscillator** and a very long, deep decay.[11]
- **TR-909**: instead uses a more synthetic hybrid approach with a pitched oscillator, a controlled pitch sweep, and an added click/transient layer.[3][5][8]

So the key difference is that the **808 is the more resonant, bridged-T / long-decay style bass drum**, while the **909 is the punchier, more controlled, attack-heavy hybrid kick**.[3][11]

## Sources used

- Sound On Sound, *Practical Bass Drum Synthesis* — https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/practical-bass-drum-synthesis[3]
- Sound On Sound, *Synthesizing Drums: The Bass Drum* — https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/synthesizing-drums-bass-drum[11]
- Roland Cloud TR-909 manual PDF — https://www.rolandcloud.com/getmedia/a88fc05f-0b9f-4ba2-8266-b2272ba31572/TR-909-Manual-E.pdf?ext=.pdf[4]
- Roland support, TR-909 technical specifications — https://support.roland.com/hc/en-us/articles/201921899-TR-909-Technical-Specifications[8]
- Colin Fraser, TR909 sound mods — http://www.colinfraser.com/tr909/909mods/909mods.htm[2]
- TR-909 sound mods PDF — https://www.firstpr.com.au/rwi/tr-909/TR-909-Sound-Mods.pdf[5]
- Roland TR-909 service manual — https://device.report/m/e68d6d4f34518bd188bc37ac59ceee7b35fab3b2e551f00c8891a15e15539263.pdf[1]

If you want, I can turn this into a **spec-sheet style table** with “parameter / likely numeric range / source / confidence” and separate **909 stock** vs **modded 909** vs **808**.
